newsitem.title: USA: Outlook grows gloomy for U.S. Treasuries -- charts.
newsitem.headline: Outlook grows gloomy for U.S. Treasuries -- charts.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are expected to stay rangebound over the next two weeks but chart analysts said the technical outlook for government securities has grown bleaker after last week's sharp sell-off.
"People are going to try to sell upticks ... I think the bears control the ball," said Michael Strauss, managing director and chief technical strategist at Chase Securities.
Benchmark 30-year T-bond prices fell sharply last week after surprisingly strong economic data, a gloomier technical scenario and mutual fund unloading triggered a large sell-off.
The selling boosted the bond yield to levels around 6.98 percent from 6.80 percent seen early last week and the 6.69 percent registered in the beginning of the month.
The downturn showed players rejected most of the early August rally that followed the release of friendly industry and employment data for July, increasing the odds for a bear market ahead.
"At a minimum, the scenario is slightly bleaker and it's potentially much worse," said Joel Marver, chief technical analyst at Technical Data.
"You have re-entered that four-month band ... which is centered at 7.0 percent or even a little higher," he added.
Long-term yields are now seen trading in a range between 7.00/7.10 percent and 6.80/6.90 percent.
Analysts said the market may reach the higher end of that band and then stop to catch its breath. But the underlying trend, they added, remains bearish.
"We could stabilize a little around 7.0 percent. But if we do pierce those levels, we could easily move towards 7.20/7.25 percent," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
Technical analysts said, however, the market has proven over the last few months that it has a strong resistance barrier in the 7.10/7.20 percent area.

"The market did seem to form really good support towards 7.10 to 7.20 percent. That has been formed since April. We've tested that ... at least three times," said Walter Burke, senior technical analyst at MCM MoneyWatch Inc.
Despite the recent back up in yields over the last week, some analysts said short-end yields remain below levels seen about a month ago, indicating a temporary oversold condition.
The market is gearing up for the sale of $18.75 billion of two-year notes Tuesday with the securities changing hands at around 6.18 percent in Monday's midday when-issued trading.
At last month's auction, those same securities were placed with a yield of around 6.28 percent.
"We're a little bit oversold short term. The market may try to stabilize but I question how far the upside will go," Strauss said. "I do expect higher rates going forward."

Letting alone the rivalry between technicians and fundamental economists, analysts said the market is bracing for some key data that could have a large impact on the performance of bond, note and bill charts.

The market is now waiting for the National Association of Purchasing Management index and the employment report on September 3 and 6, respectively. Both indicators are for August. The data are seen as crucial to help the Federal Reserve define the future course of monetary policy at the September 24 meeting of its policy-setting arm.
